Metric definitions
Composite score
Power profile combined with game-day opportunity, 1–100. Rewards power hitters who are overdue for a home run; flags batters whose results exceed their expected stats.
Baseline score
Raw batter power profile from a rolling Statcast window: barrel%, hard-hit%, xSLG, fly-ball%, HR/FB and contact trend. On live data each rate is regressed toward the league mean by sample size. The window is 30 days, not the 14 the metric is usually quoted over — backtesting found 14 days (~26 batted balls) far too short for a rate to stabilise, and 30 days (~55) measurably better at ranking.
Matchup context
Handedness splits, pitch-arsenal fit and spray-angle-versus-fence-distance are computed and shown on each player card, but carry no weight in the composite: backtesting found they add nothing once the underlying rates are properly estimated.
xSLG
Expected slugging on contact — averaged over batted balls only, with strikeouts excluded from the denominator. It therefore runs far above the familiar season figure and can exceed 1.000. Actual SLG is computed on the same denominator so the two are directly comparable.
Opportunity score
Game-day context for this matchup: opposing pitcher HR vulnerability, park factor, wind, temperature and lineup position. 50 is neutral.
On the flags
These are checked against 25,721 logged batter-games, and the test is deliberately unkind: a flag only counts if the batters it marks homer more often than their own score already predicts. Once you account for that, DUE, Heating and OVERPERFORMING add nothing — their apparent lift was “these are high-scoring batters”. They stayed on the board because they explain what the row is, and they are labelled that way rather than implying an edge. The same test did find real information in batting order and in a thin batted-ball sample — so that was fixed in the score itself rather than left as a flag to work around: the batting-order weight went from 12 to 34, and park, wind and temperature were corrected the same way. On the current corpus no flag departs from its score by more than chance, in either of two seasons. See HR outcome findings.md.
DUE
Descriptive, not predictive. A power hitter in an HR drought whose contact metrics are strong: high barrel rate, strong hard-hit rate, low HR/FB. It tells you why the row looks interesting — it does not mean he is more likely to homer tonight. Measured over 25,721 batter-games, DUE rows homered at 0.88× the rate their own composite score implies (95% CI 0.69–1.12), so the chip carries no information the score does not already have. Kept as a label, not as an edge.
OVERPERFORMING
Actual results exceed expected stats (xSLG, xBA). Measured at 1.04× the rate the score implies (95% CI 0.95–1.15) — the interval contains 1, so treat it as a description of what has happened rather than a forecast that it will stop.
Heating
Descriptive, not predictive. Rising barrel rate plus several games without a home run. Measured over the same 25,721 batter-games, Heating rows homered at 0.89× the rate their score implies (95% CI 0.76–1.05) — no better than the score alone. Recent form does not predict home runs here: a rising barrel trend and a falling one produce the same rate, at both a 14-day and a 21-day window. Sorted by barrel trend so you can see the form; not because the form is worth anything.
Barrel %
Share of batted balls with optimal exit velocity (98+ mph) and launch angle (26–30°). League average ~7%, elite 15%+.
Park factor
Stadium HR-friendliness vs league average, 100 = neutral. Yankee Stadium 119, Coors 117, Great American 115, Oracle Park 82.
Rank movement
Change vs the previous day's board. Green up = climbed, red down = dropped, NEW = unranked yesterday, dash = unchanged.
Scoring weights live in SCORING and the data generator is buildSampleSlate(), both in app.js.
